vignette:
Sanjay, a 68-year-old South Asian man, had been a dedicated non-profit worker for decades, but his life irrevocably shifted after a home invasion last year. He was brutally raped, an experience that left him with a profound sense of defilement and an inability to articulate the horror-he knows what happened but struggles to find words to describe it. Even now, when memories of the assault flood back, he sometimes hears the intruder's hushed threats and feels the searing physical pain in his body as if it were happening all over again. These intrusive memories make him certain he is a lousy coper; he believes his reactions since the event prove he is fundamentally broken, that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again, shaping his experience of memories as overwhelming and unmanageable. To escape these relentless replays, he had started engaging in self-harm, a desperate attempt to create a physical pain that might drown out the mental agony. This conviction that he is a bad coper, unable to manage his own mind or feelings, drives him to desperate measures. When the overwhelming feelings become too much, Sanjay finds himself hurting himself physically, a a desperate attempt to release the unbearable internal pressure.

His persistent belief that he is permanently an outsider now, fundamentally changed and isolated, also fuels a pervasive sense of threat. He is constantly on high alert, listening for any unexpected or loud sounds, his body tensing, convinced they signal danger. This hypervigilance, particularly the constant listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering his home, confirms his darkest fears about the world and reinforces his appraisal that he is an outsider, perpetually unsafe. When someone touches him unexpectedly, even a colleague's hand on his shoulder in the busy non-profit office, he reacts with alarm, a jolt of terror shooting through him, often triggered by a memory of the assault, further solidifying his belief that he is an outsider, unable to connect normally with others. These moments of intense threat lead him to engage in a range of maladaptive strategies. For example, he insists on always sitting with his back against a wall, needing to see the entire room, whether he's in a work meeting or a cafe. This strategy, meant to keep him safe, paradoxically increases his anxiety when he can't find such a spot, leaving him feeling even more exposed and vulnerable, thus heightening his overall sense of threat.

His strategies, though intended to protect him, have become a cage. Avoiding being alone in his apartment or office, he often stays late at work or visits friends, unable to face the silence of his own space. When he is alone, the memories of what happened become particularly vivid, making him feel the pain and hear the sounds of the assault more intensely. Yet, these avoidance behaviors only solidify his belief that he is a lousy coper, unable to handle even basic solitude, and reinforces the idea that he is permanently an outsider. The constant effort to maintain these safety behaviors, like meticulously scanning a room for a safe seat, is exhausting and leaves him drained. This constant mental effort to keep the trauma at bay, to not think about it, meant the memories never truly settled, always remaining fresh and raw, ready to erupt with full force. What finally brought Sanjay to seek help was the realization that his life had shrunk to the point where he was merely surviving, not living. He feared he would spend the rest of his days trapped in this cycle, forever an outsider, never feeling normal emotions again. This belief that he was permanently broken and unable to feel normal emotions often pulled his mind back to the exact moment of the assault, as if he were replaying it to find the source of his irreparable damage.

- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette does not show how Sanjay's maladaptive strategies directly influence or lead to changes in his memories.

  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
